docs.title: Home
docs.text:
RISICO

RISICO (Rischio Incendi E Coordinamento) is the wildfire danger forecasting model developed by CIMA Research Foundation and used operationally by the Italian Civil Protection. From a weather forecast and maps of vegetation and terrain, it computes hour by hour how dry the vegetation is and how fast and how intensely a fire would spread on every cell of a map.

Try it in your browser Get started How it works Developer guide API reference

docs.title: What you can do with it
docs.text:
• Forecast fire danger over a region or a country: run it every day on a weather forecast and get maps of fuel moisture, rate of spread and fireline intensity for the coming days.
  • Compare indices: the same run computes the Canadian Fire Weather Index and eight more indices used around the world (Keetch–Byram, McArthur Mark 5, Angström, Fosberg, Nesterov, Sharples, Orieux, Hot–Dry–Windy). See Fire Danger Indices.
  • Study past seasons: run it on weather reanalyses or archived forecasts.
  • Embed the models in your own Rust program, without the files: see the Developer Guide.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
risico-2023 is the current implementation of RISICO, written in Rust:

  • one command-line program, with no external libraries to install;
  • NetCDF weather inputs and outputs, GeoTIFF land data, plus GeoTIFF, Zarr and PNG outputs;
  • domains of any size in bounded memory, from one cell to a continent (Large Domains and Performance);
  • a Rust library with the models alone (API reference);
  • a WebAssembly build of the same program, which runs the interactive demo in your browser.

The source code is on GitHub.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. See it: the interactive demo runs the real model on one cell or on a map of Liguria, in your browser, with nothing to install.
  2. Understand it: How RISICO Works explains weather inputs, land data, warm state and outputs.
  3. Run it: Getting Started installs the program and runs it on the sample data shipped with the repository.
  4. Use your data: Input Data and Configuration describe how to set up your own domain.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
The API reference is generated from the source with rustdoc and published with this site:

Open the API reference

It documents the risico library crate, the models without the runner. Start from the crate page: it explains the concepts and units, with a tested example. The main modules:

Module Contents risico::models::input Input, InputElement: the weather of one timestamp; InputVariableName: the variable names of input files risico::models::output Output, OutputElement, OutputVariableName: the output variables of every model risico::modules::risico RISICO: properties, vegetation, warm state, state, the legacy / v2023 / v2025 formulations risico::modules::fwi Canadian FWI System: properties, warm state, state, the legacy / cffdrs / sliding_window formulations risico::modules All models: KBDI, Mark 5, Angström, Fosberg, Nesterov, Sharples, Orieux, HDW risico::config The configuration.yml schema (feature config) risico::constants Shared constants, among them NODATAVAL

To build it locally:

cargo doc --no-deps --lib --open

For a guided tour with complete programs see the Programmatic Workflow.

docs.title: CLI Usage
docs.text:
The repository builds four commands:

Command Purpose risico-2023 Run the models of a configuration on a set of weather inputs streaming-inspect Validate a configuration and print its tile plan, without running static-converter Convert the text static data of the previous RISICO implementation to GeoTIFF layers warm-state-converter Convert the text warm states of the previous RISICO implementation to NetCDF snapshots

Most users need only risico-2023. The two converters are for existing installations of the previous RISICO implementation (see Converting Legacy Data).

cargo build --release --bins    # builds all four in target/release/

Every command prints its usage with --help.

docs.title: risico-2023
docs.text:
Usage: risico-2023 <DATE> <CONFIG_PATH> <INPUT_PATH>

Arguments:
  <DATE>         Model date in the format YYYYMMDDHHMM
  <CONFIG_PATH>  Path to the configuration file
  <INPUT_PATH>   Path to the input data file

Options:
  -h, --help     Print help
  -V, --version  Print version

docs.title: Arguments
docs.text: DATE The run date, in UTC. Each model starts from the warm-state snapshot of the day before (see Configuration), and output times are counted from it. Every timestamp of the inputs is processed, so give inputs that start after that snapshot. CONFIG_PATH A YAML configuration: the models to run, their static data, warm state and outputs (see Configuration). INPUT_PATH Either a directory of NetCDF weather files (every .nc file in it is read, see Input Data) or a text file listing .zbin files of the previous RISICO implementation, one per line.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
./target/release/risico-2023 \
  202607010000 \
  /opt/risico/configuration.yml \
  /data/weather/20260701/

A run reads the static data and warm state of every model, then streams the inputs one timestamp at a time through each tile of each model, writing outputs at the configured hours and the warm state at warm_state_hour (see Large Domains and Performance).

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Variable Default Effect RUST_LOG info Log level: error, warn, info, debug, trace. Logs go to standard error. TMPDIR /tmp Base of the scratch directory when the configuration sets none.

The command exits with a non-zero status and an error message when the configuration, the static data or the inputs cannot be read.

docs.title: streaming-inspect
docs.text:
Checks a configuration without reading any weather: it loads the static data, resolves every model and prints the tile plan the runner would use. Useful before deploying a new configuration, or to try other tile sizes.

Usage: streaming-inspect [OPTIONS] <DATE> <CONFIG>

Arguments:
  <DATE>    Model date in YYYYMMDDHHMM form
  <CONFIG>  YAML or legacy text configuration

Options:
      --tile-height <TILE_HEIGHT>        Override raster tile height
      --tile-width <TILE_WIDTH>          Override raster tile width
      --cells-per-tile <CELLS_PER_TILE>  Override legacy cells per tile

./target/release/streaming-inspect 202607010000 configuration.yml --tile-height 256 --tile-width 256

docs.title: static-converter
docs.text:
Converts the legacy regular-grid static files to the aligned GeoTIFF layers the model reads (see Converting Legacy Data).

Usage: static-converter risico [OPTIONS] --cells <CELLS> --grid <GRID> --output <OUTPUT>
      --cells <CELLS>    RISICO cell file: lon lat slope aspect vegetation
      --grid <GRID>      Legacy grid file (GRIDNROWS=, MINLAT=, ...)
      --output <OUTPUT>  Destination directory for the GeoTIFF layers
      --ppf <PPF>        Optional legacy two-column summer/winter PPF file

Usage: static-converter fwi --cells <CELLS> --grid <GRID> --output <OUTPUT>
      --cells <CELLS>    FWI cell file: lon lat
      --grid <GRID>      Legacy grid file
      --output <OUTPUT>  Destination directory for the domain mask

docs.title: warm-state-converter
docs.text:
Converts legacy text warm states to NetCDF snapshots, validated against a domain mask.

Usage: warm-state-converter config [OPTIONS] --config <CONFIG> --model-name <MODEL_NAME> --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX>
      --config <CONFIG>                Migrated YAML configuration containing GeoTIFF and NetCDF warm-state settings
      --model-name <MODEL_NAME>        `model_name` of the model entry to convert, as it appears in the config file
      --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX>  Legacy filename prefix, or a directory when files are named only by timestamp
      --latest-only                    Convert only the newest legacy snapshot
      --overwrite                      Replace an existing NetCDF snapshot with the same timestamp

Usage: warm-state-converter risico|fwi [OPTIONS] --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX> --domain-mask <DOMAIN_MASK> --output <OUTPUT> --model-version <MODEL_VERSION>
      --legacy-prefix <LEGACY_PREFIX>  Legacy filename prefix, or a directory when files are named only by timestamp
      --domain-mask <DOMAIN_MASK>      GeoTIFF domain mask used to validate cell count and define the output grid
      --output <OUTPUT>                Destination directory for NetCDF snapshots
      --model-version <MODEL_VERSION>  Model version stored in and validated against each snapshot
      --latest-only                    Convert only the newest legacy snapshot
      --overwrite                      Replace an existing NetCDF snapshot with the same timestamp

The config form takes paths and model metadata from a configuration that already points at the GeoTIFF static data and the NetCDF warm-state directory; the risico and fwi forms take them explicitly.

docs.title: How RISICO Works
docs.text: This page explains the ideas behind a RISICO run: what goes in, what comes out, and how one day's run hands over to the next. Read it before preparing your own data.

docs.title: Fire danger, not fire spread
docs.text:
RISICO does not simulate a fire. It estimates, for every cell of a map and every hour, how easily a fire would start and spread there if one were ignited: how dry the dead vegetation is, how fast a flame front would advance and how much energy it would release. Civil protection services use these maps to decide where to raise alert levels, pre-position resources or restrict activities.

The numbers come from two kinds of information:

  • weather, which changes every hour: temperature, humidity, wind, rain and snow;
  • the land, which does not: vegetation type, slope and aspect of the terrain.

docs.title: The pieces of a run
docs.text:
┌───────────────────────┐
 weather inputs ─▶                       ├─▶ outputs (maps of each variable, hour by hour)
 static data    ─▶   risico-2023 run     │
 warm state     ─▶                       ├─▶ new warm state (for the next run)
                 └───────────────────────┘
                     configuration.yml
Run date The date and time a run is for, in UTC, written YYYYMMDDHHMM. It selects the warm state to start from and names some outputs. It does not filter the weather: every timestamp in the inputs is processed. Weather inputs Gridded fields, normally a weather forecast, one value per grid point and timestamp: temperature, relative humidity (or dew point), wind, rain and optionally snow cover. They are read from NetCDF files. Their grid can be coarser than the model's: each model cell takes the value of the nearest weather grid point. See Input Data. Static data Maps that describe the land, all on the same grid: a domain mask saying which cells to compute, and for RISICO the slope, aspect and vegetation type of each cell. They are GeoTIFF files. The grid of the static data is the grid the model computes on: the Italian operational setup uses 1 km cells. Warm state The memory of the model. Dead vegetation dries and wets slowly, so the moisture of one hour depends on all the weather before it. At the end of each day, a run saves the state of every cell (a snapshot) and the next run starts from it. Without a snapshot the model starts from default values and needs a few days of weather before its results are meaningful: this is called spin-up. Outputs Maps of the variables you ask for, written at the times you ask for, on an output grid of your choice (the native grid, or a coarser one). NetCDF is the usual format; GeoTIFF, Zarr, PNG and a legacy binary format are also available. Configuration A YAML file listing the models to run and, for each, where its static data, warm state and outputs are. See Configuration.

docs.title: The daily cycle
docs.text:
An operational chain runs once a day, when the new weather forecast arrives:

  1. The forecast for the coming days is converted to NetCDF.
  2. risico-2023 runs with today's date. Each model loads the snapshot saved by yesterday's run, steps through the forecast hour by hour and writes its maps.
  3. During the run, the model saves a new snapshot at the configured hour (warm_state_hour, midnight UTC by default) of each day it goes through.
  4. Tomorrow's run starts from the snapshot saved today.

By default a run on date D looks for the snapshot of D minus one day, or the newest one before it, up to five days old (warm_state_lag_days and max_age_hours change this). It never starts from a snapshot written later than that, so running the same day twice gives the same result.

docs.title: What RISICO computes
docs.text:
For each cell, every hour, RISICO:

  1. updates the dead fine fuel moisture (dffm, %), the water content of dead leaves, needles and twigs: dry and warm air, wind and sun lower it, rain raises it;
  2. computes the rate of spread (V, m/h) a fire front would have in that vegetation, higher on dry fuel, with the wind and uphill;
  3. computes the fireline intensity (I, kW/m), the energy a fire front would release, from the rate of spread and the fuel load of the vegetation.

The vegetation types and their parameters (fuel load, heat content, base spread rate and moisture response) come from a vegetation catalogue, a small text table shipped with the static data. Two optional seasonal layers, PPF (summer and winter), weight spread and intensity by how fire-prone each area is in each season.

The same run can also compute the Canadian Fire Weather Index and eight more fire danger indices used around the world, from the same weather.

docs.title: Cells, grids and tiles
docs.text:
The model computes on cells: the pixels of the domain mask that are active. Inactive pixels (sea, outside the country) are skipped and get no value in the outputs.

To keep memory bounded on large domains, a run processes the domain in rectangular tiles, timestamp by timestamp. This is automatic; Large Domains and Performance shows how to tune it.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Aspect Direction a slope faces, in degrees clockwise from north Cell One pixel of the domain mask where the model computes Domain mask GeoTIFF whose non-zero pixels are the cells to compute dffm Dead fine fuel moisture, % of dry weight Fireline intensity Energy released per metre of fire front, kW/m FWI Canadian Fire Weather Index System PPF Seasonal weighting layers of spread and intensity (summer and winter) Rate of spread Speed a fire front would advance, m/h Run date Date and time a run is for, UTC Spin-up Days of weather a model needs before its state is realistic Snapshot Saved warm state at one time, a NetCDF file Static data Maps that do not change during a run: mask, slope, aspect, vegetation Warm state Model memory carried from one run to the next zbin Binary input and output format of the previous RISICO implementation

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: A run is described by one YAML file: which models to run, where their data are and which outputs to write. This page is the reference of that file. The sample configuration is a complete, working example to start from.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
models:                       # required: the models to run, one entry each
  - type: RISICO
    ...
  - type: FWI
    ...
palettes: {}                  # required: colour palettes for PNG outputs ({} if none)
netcdf_input_configuration:   # optional: names used in the weather files
  ...
streaming:                    # optional: memory and performance tuning
  ...
Key Content See models List of model entries below palettes Map from output variable name to a palette file, for PNGWJSON outputs Outputs netcdf_input_configuration Variable, coordinate and time names of the weather files, when they differ from the defaults Input Data streaming Tile size, memory budget, scratch directory Large Domains and Performance

Relative paths are resolved from the directory the command is run in.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
A RISICO entry, with every key:

models:
  - type: RISICO
    model_name: RISICO
    model_version: v2025
    static_data:
      type: geotiff
      domain_mask: static/domain_mask.tif
      slope: static/slope.tif
      aspect: static/aspect.tif
      vegetation_id: static/vegetation_id.tif
      vegetation_catalog: static/p_vegetazione.csv
      ppf_summer: static/ppf_summer.tif      # optional, with ppf_winter
      ppf_winter: static/ppf_winter.tif
    warm_state:
      type: netcdf
      directory: state/RISICO
      max_age_hours: 120
      on_missing: error
    warm_state_hour: 0
    warm_state_lag_days: 1
    output_time_resolution: 1
    output_types:
      - ...                                  # see Outputs
Key Meaning Default type The model: RISICO, FWI, or one of the other indices required model_name A name for the entry, used in the logs required model_version The formulation, see Fire Danger Indices required (RISICO, FWI and some others) static_data The land data, below required (RISICO, FWI) warm_state Where snapshots are read and written, below required (RISICO, FWI) warm_state_hour Hour of the day (UTC) at which a snapshot is saved 0 warm_state_lag_days How many days before the run date the snapshot to start from is 1 output_time_resolution Hours between two written outputs, counted from the run date required for RISICO; 24 for FWI output_time_offset FWI only: hours from the run date of the first daily output 0 output_types The outputs, below required

The other indices take cells_file_path (their cells, see Input Data) instead of static_data, and warm_state_path (a file name prefix) instead of warm_state when they have a memory.

An FWI entry needs only the domain mask:

  - type: FWI
    model_name: FWI
    model_version: cffdrs
    static_data:
      type: geotiff
      domain_mask: static/domain_mask.tif
    warm_state:
      type: netcdf
      directory: state/FWI
      on_missing: defaults
    output_time_resolution: 24
    output_time_offset: 12
    output_types:
      - ...

docs.title: Static data
docs.text: static_data lists the GeoTIFF layers described in Input Data. type is always geotiff; domain_mask is required, the RISICO layers are required for RISICO, and the two PPF layers are optional but go together. The domain mask defines the grid the model computes on and the cells it computes.

docs.title: Warm state
docs.text:
Key Meaning Default type Always netcdf required directory Directory of the snapshots; created if missing required max_age_hours Oldest snapshot accepted, in hours before the time searched 120 on_missing What to do when no snapshot is found: error stops the run, defaults starts from default values error

A snapshot is saved at warm_state_hour of every day the run goes through, as <directory>/RISICO_YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ.nc (or FWI_...). Give each model its own directory.

To start, a run looks for the snapshot at the run date minus warm_state_lag_days, plus warm_state_hour; if there is none, it takes the newest older one within max_age_hours. Snapshots record the model version and are rejected if it differs. They are NetCDF grids with latitude and longitude, so they can be opened like any output; when the static grid changes resolution, the state is resampled onto the new grid.

Use on_missing: defaults for the first run of a new setup, then switch to error so that a broken chain stops instead of silently restarting from defaults.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Each model lists any number of output_types. An output type is a set of variables written in one format, on one grid, into one directory:

    output_types:
      - internal_name: RISICO
        name: RISICO
        path: output/RISICO
        format: NETCDF
        compression_level: 4
        grid:
          nrows: 103
          ncols: 274
          min_lat: 43.704665
          max_lat: 44.749078
          min_lon: 7.403763
          max_lon: 10.199103
        variables:
          - { internal_name: dffm, name: dffm, cluster_mode: Mean, precision: -1 }
          - { internal_name: V,    name: V,    cluster_mode: Max,  precision: 0 }
Key Meaning internal_name, name Names of the output type, used in logs and file names path Output directory, created if missing format NETCDF, GEOTIFF, ZARR, PNGWJSON or ZBIN, below compression_level NETCDF: deflate level 0–9; ZARR: zstd level 0–22. Default 7 grid The output grid: nrows × ncols cell centres from min_lat/min_lon to max_lat/max_lon, both included grid_path Instead of grid: a text grid file of the previous RISICO implementation variables The variables to write

Each variable has:

Key Meaning internal_name The model variable, as listed in Fire Danger Indices name Its name in the output files cluster_mode How the model cells falling in one output pixel are combined: Mean, Min or Max precision Values are rounded to a multiple of 10precision: -1 keeps one decimal, 0 rounds to units, 1 to tens

The output grid does not have to match the model grid: a coarser grid aggregates cells with cluster_mode, which is how a 1 km run produces a 5 km map. Use the domain mask's own grid to write every cell.

Outputs are written every output_time_resolution hours from the run date: 1 writes every hour, 24 once a day at the hour of the run date (shifted by output_time_offset for FWI).

docs.title: Formats
docs.text: format What is written NETCDF One NetCDF-4 file per variable, <path>/<name>.nc, with time, latitude and longitude axes and one map per output time. Readable once the run has finished. GEOTIFF One GeoTIFF per variable and output time ZARR One Zarr v3 store per variable, <path>/<name>.zarr, same axes as NetCDF PNGWJSON One coloured PNG image per variable and output time, with a JSON file describing its georeference, for web maps. Needs a palette per variable. ZBIN The binary format of the previous RISICO implementation

docs.title: PNG palettes
docs.text:
PNGWJSON outputs colour each variable with the palette named after the variable's name:

palettes:
  V: palettes/RISICO_V.pal
  I: palettes/RISICO_I.pal

A palette file has one line per class: the lower bound of the class and the red, green, blue and alpha values (0–255), separated by tabs:

-9999   200 200 200 0
0   0   153 255 255
68  0   128 0   255
104 255 255 0   255

docs.title: Checking a configuration
docs.text: streaming-inspect reads a configuration and its static data and warm state and reports what a run would do, without reading weather or writing anything (see CLI Usage).

docs.title: Converting Legacy Data
docs.text:
Only for existing RISICO installations

This page is for operators of the previous RISICO implementation, whose static data, grids and warm states are text files. New setups prepare GeoTIFF static data directly (see Input Data) and can skip it.

The previous implementation describes the land as a text file of cells (lon lat slope aspect vegetation per line) with a separate grid file, and saves its warm state as text files. The two converters below turn them, once, into the GeoTIFF layers and NetCDF snapshots this version reads.

docs.title: Static data
docs.text:
Convert existing regular-grid static files with the offline static-converter utility, which writes single-band EPSG:4326 GeoTIFF layers. The converter detects, per axis, whether legacy bounds represent outer edges or cell centres; this accommodates the conventions used by the deployed grids.

cargo run --release --bin static-converter -- risico \
  --cells /share/risico/RISICO2023/STATIC/risico2023_input_1km.txt \
  --grid /share/risico/RISICO2023/GRID/input_1km_GRID.txt \
  --output /opt/risico/RISICO2023/STATIC/geotiff

cargo run --release --bin static-converter -- fwi \
  --cells /share/risico/FWIWORLD/STATIC/FWI_world.txt \
  --grid /share/risico/FWIWORLD/GRID/GRID.txt \
  --output /opt/risico/FWIWORLD/STATIC/geotiff

The converter checks that cells are unique and in the canonical north-to-south, west-to-east order. This keeps legacy state rows aligned during a progressive migration.

For warm-state-converter, --legacy-prefix may name a prefix or a directory whose files are bare YYYYMMDDHHMM timestamps. Every written snapshot is read back and validated before conversion is reported as successful. A malformed legacy file is reported without preventing other discovered snapshots from being checked.

docs.title: Warm state
docs.text:
Existing legacy snapshots can be converted before cutover. The domain mask defines the output NetCDF grid and places each text row at its corresponding active pixel. By default all timestamped files matching the prefix are converted; existing NetCDF files are skipped unless --overwrite is used.

cargo run --bin warm-state-converter -- config \
  --config /opt/risico/configuration.yml \
  --model-name RISICO2023 \
  --legacy-prefix /opt/risico/STATE0/state0RISICO_ \
  --latest-only

# The explicit form is useful outside a migrated deployment:
cargo run --bin warm-state-converter -- risico \
  --legacy-prefix /opt/risico/STATE0/state0RISICO_ \
  --domain-mask /opt/risico/static/domain_mask.tif \
  --output /opt/risico/state-nc \
  --model-version v2025

cargo run --bin warm-state-converter -- fwi \
  --legacy-prefix /opt/risico/STATE0/state0FWI_ \
  --domain-mask /opt/risico/static/domain_mask.tif \
  --output /opt/risico/state-nc \
  --model-version legacy \
  --latest-only

docs.title: Interactive Demo
docs.text:
This page runs the real RISICO program in your browser, with nothing to install: the same risico-2023 used operationally, compiled to WebAssembly. It covers a 1 km grid over Liguria, in north-western Italy. Your browser prepares the input files, runs the model and draws its outputs; no data is sent to a server.

Three levels, from a single cell to a regional map:

  1. One cell, your weather. Pick a cell on the map, set a weather scenario with the sliders and, if you like, change its vegetation, slope and aspect. Nothing is downloaded: all ten models run on one cell in well under a second.
  2. One cell, real weather. The same cell driven by real hourly weather: July 2025, bundled with the page as a NetCDF file, or today's analysis and forecast from Open-Meteo.
  3. Liguria at 1 km. RISICO and FWI on the 16 000 cells of a Liguria cut-out of the Italian domain, with the same choice of weather on a 0.125° grid. Browse the maps in time and click a cell for its series.

docs.title: 1 · One cell, your weather
docs.text:
Click any cell of the map: the panel shows its vegetation, slope and aspect, read from the land data. Set a weather scenario (start date, length, mean temperature and daily range, humidity, wind, a rain event) and, if you like, override the vegetation class, slope and aspect. Run all indices runs the ten models on that cell.

The results come as interactive charts, grouped by model: the weather actually used, RISICO hourly (fine fuel moisture, rate of spread, intensity, wind and temperature effects), the FWI moisture codes and behaviour indices, and every other index.

docs.title: 2 · One cell, real weather
docs.text: The same cell with real hourly weather. By default the page uses its July 2025 sample, a NetCDF input bundled with the site, so nothing is requested from outside: pick the first day and the length of the period. Alternatively, Today requests the analysis of up to two months before now and up to ten days of forecast from Open-Meteo; a dashed line marks the current time.

docs.title: 3 · Liguria at 1 km
docs.text:
RISICO and FWI on every cell of the domain, on any period of the July 2025 sample (a week takes a few seconds) or on today's forecast. When the run ends, pick a variable and move through time with the slider; the legend uses the operational palettes.

Click a cell for its full series of the selected variable:

About this demo

In the browser the model runs on one processor core; the installed program uses all of them. Every run starts from default moisture, with no warm state, and spins up on the first days of weather. That is enough for the fine fuel moisture of RISICO, but slow codes such as the FWI drought code (DC) or KBDI need months to settle. Mark 5 and KBDI use a mean annual rainfall of 800 mm and Orieux a heat index of 70 for every cell.

The July 2025 sample comes from the Open-Meteo historical forecast archive and is served with the site; weather data by Open-Meteo.com, licensed under CC BY 4.0; the same files run with the command-line model, see Run the sample. Today's weather is requested by your browser from Open-Meteo's free API: 2 m temperature and humidity, 10 m wind, precipitation and snow depth. The free tier allows about 600 locations a minute; the Liguria map needs about 200, and the page waits and retries if the limit is reached.

See Building the Web Demo for how the bundle is built.

docs.title: Large Domains and Performance
docs.text: risico-2023 runs domains of any size, from a few cells to a continent, in bounded memory. The defaults suit most runs; this page explains how a run is organised and how to tune it when the domain is large or the machine is small.

docs.title: How a run is organised
docs.text:
A run never holds the whole domain's time series in memory. It splits the domain into rectangular tiles and goes through the weather one timestamp at a time; at each timestamp it steps every tile, then writes that timestamp's outputs. Every model uses the same runner.

In detail, for each configured model:

  1. Build a spatial tile plan, gather every tile's immutable properties once, seed every tile's live state from the warm state, and register each tile's input coordinates. The whole-domain property and warm-state arrays are released at this point.
  2. Process the input timeline in timestamp order, decoding each timestamp's source fields once.
  3. Within each timestamp, run every tile through the model: its state is either kept in memory or restored from its checkpoint, as tile_state decides.
  4. Write the tile's requested native variables into the current timestamp's plane-oriented, little-endian output scratch file and, when the state is on disk, checkpoint its updated state.
  5. After all tiles complete that timestamp, resample its native variables onto each configured output grid, encode NETCDF, ZBIN, ZARR, PNGWJSON or GEOTIFF output, and remove the scratch file. Independent output variables may be postprocessed in parallel, and the whole step may run in the background while the next timestamp is stepped.
  6. Assemble any scheduled warm-state records in canonical model-cell order and write the model's NetCDF (or, for the text-file indices, text) snapshot, in the same background step as the output.

Raster-backed models use clipped rectangular windows and omit empty windows. A window holding fewer than a quarter of a full tile's cells, as coastal and border windows do, is merged with a neighbour in its tile row, never beyond a full tile's worth of cells. Tiles are then ordered largest first so the work-stealing pool spends the tail of each timestep on the small ones. Models that read their cells from a text file use batches of cells in file order instead of windows. Both enter the same runner and model-adapter interface.

Meteorological input grids may be regular or curvilinear. Curvilinear grids retain nearest-neighbour R-tree lookup. Because source meteorological fields are normally low resolution, each decoded source field is cached whole and then sampled repeatedly for the model tiles.

GeoTIFF static layers and gridded warm-state variables are read using bounded source windows. The current configuration objects retain their compact active-cell properties and initial warm-state records; the warm state is released once every tile has been seeded from it. Exact per-tile live state, including transient accumulators and history, either stays in memory for the whole run or is checkpointed between timestamps, as tile_state decides. Decoded meteorological fields are retained while all tiles consume the current timestamp and then released. Scheduled warm-state records for the current timestamp are assembled in memory before the writer is called; native forecast output is the disk-backed portion of the pipeline.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The optional top-level streaming section of the configuration tunes the runner:

streaming:
  tile_height: 1024
  tile_width: 1024
  cells_per_tile: 1048576
  max_memory: 6GB
  tile_state: auto
  overlap_postprocess: true
  scratch_directory: /var/tmp/risico

Defaults are 512 × 512 for raster tiles and 1,048,576 cells for batches of text-file cells. scratch_directory defaults to a risico-streaming directory below the operating system's temporary directory. Tile dimensions and cells_per_tile must be greater than zero.

max_memory (for example 6GB or 768 MiB) is a target peak resident size. Tile concurrency is derived from what is left of it once the whole-domain arrays are charged, so the run adapts to the model and the domain; an explicit tile_concurrency wins over it. With neither set, one tile runs per core.

tile_state says where each tile's live state lives between timestamps:

  • auto (default): in memory when max_memory has room for every tile's state at the concurrency the run will use, or when no max_memory is set; on disk otherwise.
  • memory: always in memory. No checkpoint is written or read, which removes the largest I/O cost of a run.
  • disk: always checkpointed to the scratch directory, so only the tiles in flight hold state. This is the smallest footprint.

overlap_postprocess says whether a timestamp's output is resampled and written, and its warm state saved, while the next timestamp is being stepped. Unset, the overlap is taken when the output grids in flight and the gathered warm state still fit max_memory beside a step, or when no budget is set; true and false force it. At most one timestamp is finished in the background, so a failure there stops the run at the next timestamp.

Each model logs the decision it made and the peak it expects before the timeline starts, then logs per-timestamp phase timings (preload, step, postprocess, warm state) with the current and peak resident set size, and a total per phase at the end. streaming-inspect prints the same decision for a configuration without running it.

Output resolution does not affect numerical model execution: interpolation, clustering, precision rounding, and encoding happen only during the postprocessing stage.

See Configuration for the output formats.

Allow scratch capacity for approximately four bytes multiplied by active model cells and configured native variables, plus, when the state is on disk, the serialized live-state checkpoints and filesystem overhead. An output timestamp is held on disk only until it is postprocessed and removed; with overlap_postprocess that can be two timestamps at once.

docs.title: Inspecting a configuration
docs.text:
streaming-inspect builds each model, creates its tile plan, and instantiates the first tile's property/state adapters without running meteorological input or writing forecast output:

cargo run --bin streaming-inspect -- \
  202607240000 /opt/risico/configuration.yml \
  --tile-height 256 --tile-width 256

The inspector still performs normal configuration and warm-state validation, so the referenced static layers, palettes, and required warm snapshot must exist.

docs.title: Failure and scratch behavior
docs.text: Model failures are logged independently so another configured model may continue. Completed output scratch files are removed after successful postprocessing. If execution is interrupted or fails before cleanup, the run-specific scratch directory may remain for diagnosis and can be removed after confirming that no process is using it.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page installs risico-2023, runs it on the sample data that comes with the repository and shows how to look at the results. It takes about ten minutes. To see the model without installing anything, open the interactive demo first.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: risico-2023 is a single command-line program. It runs on Linux and macOS, and on Windows through WSL.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
You need Git and the Rust toolchain. Install Rust with rustup if cargo --version does not work:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

Then clone the repository and build:

git clone https://github.com/CIMAFoundation/risico-2023.git
cd risico-2023
cargo build --release --bin risico-2023

The first build downloads the dependencies and takes a few minutes. The program is then at target/release/risico-2023; check it with:

./target/release/risico-2023 --help

No other software is needed: NetCDF and GeoTIFF files are read and written by the program itself, without the NetCDF, HDF5 or GDAL libraries.

Prebuilt binaries

GitHub releases carry a static Linux x86_64 binary. This documentation follows the dev branch, which may be ahead of the latest release: build from source to match it.

docs.title: Run the sample
docs.text:
The repository ships a small, complete case in docs/demo/data/: the land data of a 1 km grid over Liguria, in north-western Italy, and one month of hourly weather (July 2025) over the same area.

docs/demo/data/
├── static/                        land data, 274 × 103 cells of 1 km
│   ├── domain_mask.tif            cells to compute
│   ├── slope.tif, aspect.tif      terrain
│   ├── vegetation_id.tif          vegetation type of each cell
│   ├── ppf_summer.tif, ppf_winter.tif
│   └── p_vegetazione.csv          vegetation catalogue
└── sample/
    ├── configuration.yml          runs RISICO (hourly) and FWI (daily)
    └── input/
        └── weather-2025-07.nc     hourly weather, 744 hours

Run it from the sample directory:

cd docs/demo/data/sample
../../../../target/release/risico-2023 202507010000 configuration.yml input/

The three arguments are the run date (1 July 2025, 00:00 UTC), the configuration and the directory of weather files. The run takes about 20 seconds and logs its progress. There is no warm state yet, so both models start from default values (on_missing: defaults in the configuration) and their first days are a spin-up.

When it ends, the directory holds:

output/
├── RISICO/   dffm.nc  V.nc  I.nc  T.nc  H.nc  WS.nc  P.nc     one map per hour
└── FWI/      ffmc.nc  dmc.nc  dc.nc  isi.nc  bui.nc  fwi.nc  one map per day
state/
├── RISICO/   one snapshot per day (warm state)
└── FWI/

Run it again with a later date, for example 202507150000: each model now starts from the snapshot of the day before instead of default values. That is how an operational chain runs day after day (see How RISICO Works).

docs.title: Look at the results
docs.text:
The outputs are ordinary NetCDF files with time, latitude and longitude axes:

ncdump -h output/RISICO/V.nc          # with the NetCDF tools installed

In Python, with xarray and matplotlib:

import xarray as xr

v = xr.open_dataset("output/RISICO/V.nc").V
v.sel(time="2025-07-07T15:00").plot(cmap="inferno")   # rate of spread, m/h
v.sel(latitude=44.45, longitude=8.9, method="nearest").plot()   # one cell over the month

They also open in QGIS (drag the file into the map) and in Panoply.

The variables are described in Fire Danger Indices. The ones in the sample are:

File Variable Units RISICO/dffm.nc Dead fine fuel moisture % RISICO/V.nc Rate of spread m/h RISICO/I.nc Fireline intensity kW/m RISICO/T.nc, H.nc, WS.nc, P.nc The weather the model used: temperature, humidity, wind speed, rain °C, %, m/s, mm FWI/*.nc Canadian FWI System codes and indices –

docs.title: About the sample weather
docs.text: The weather comes from the Open-Meteo historical forecast archive, on a 0.125° grid: weather data by Open-Meteo.com, licensed under CC BY 4.0. The file carries the same attribution in its attribution and license attributes. docs/demo/tools/make_sample_weather.py rebuilds it for another period. Both files are also online: the weather input and the configuration.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
To run RISICO on your own area:

  1. Read How RISICO Works for the ideas behind a run.
  2. Prepare your weather and land data as described in Input Data.
  3. Write a configuration, starting from the sample's: see Configuration.
  4. Run it as shown in CLI Usage.

Test runs on a production configuration

The output and warm-state paths of a configuration are the real destinations: a test run overwrites them. To try a change, copy the configuration and point those paths to a temporary directory.

docs.title: Fire Danger Indices
docs.text:
Besides RISICO, risico-2023 computes the Canadian Fire Weather Index System and eight more fire danger indices used in different countries. They all read the same weather inputs, so one run can compare them on the same domain. The interactive demo runs all of them on one cell, side by side, and References lists the publication behind each.

Each model is one entry of the configuration's models list; its type selects the model. The variable names in the tables are the internal_names an output lists (see Configuration).

docs.title: Weather each model uses
docs.text:
Model Temperature Humidity Wind speed Wind direction Rain Snow cover RISICO ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ optional FWI ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Mark 5 ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ KBDI ✓ ✓ Angström ✓ ✓ Fosberg ✓ ✓ ✓ Nesterov ✓ ✓ (dew point) ✓ Sharples ✓ ✓ ✓ Orieux ✓ ✓ ✓ Hot–Dry–Windy ✓ ✓ (vapour pressure deficit) ✓

Humidity can be given as relative humidity, dew point or specific humidity; the dew point and the vapour pressure deficit are derived from what is given (see Input Data).

docs.title: RISICO
docs.text:
type: RISICO. Developed by CIMA Research Foundation and used operationally by the Italian Civil Protection. RISICO follows the moisture of the dead fine fuel hour by hour, drying it with temperature, humidity and wind and wetting it with rain, and turns it into the rate of spread and the intensity a fire would have in the vegetation of each cell, corrected for wind and slope (see How RISICO Works). The model is described by Fiorucci et al. (2008) and, in its current version, by Perello et al. (2025): see References.

Model versions (model_version):

  • v2025: the current formulation: the moisture equations of v2023, with a revised rate of spread and weather effect;
  • v2023: revised dead fuel moisture equations and rate of spread;
  • legacy: the original equations. An unknown version also selects them.

Static data: domain mask, slope, aspect, vegetation id and catalogue, and optionally the summer and winter PPF layers. Warm state: yes.

Variable Meaning Units dffm Dead fine fuel moisture % V Rate of spread m/h I Fireline intensity kW/m W Wind effect on spread (multiplier) – contrT Temperature effect on spread (multiplier) – VPPF, IPPF Spread and intensity weighted by the seasonal PPF layer m/h, kW/m NDVI, NDWI Satellite vegetation and water factors – VNDWI, INDWI, VNDVI, INDVI Spread and intensity with the satellite factors m/h, kW/m VPPFNDWI, IPPFNDWI, VPPFNDVI, IPPFNDVI With both PPF and satellite factors m/h, kW/m

The weather the model actually used can be written too: temperature (°C), humidity (%), windSpeed (m/s), windDir, rain (mm) and snowCover (cm).

docs.title: Canadian Fire Weather Index System
docs.text:
type: FWI. The Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System (Van Wagner, 1987), the most widely used fire danger rating system in the world. Three moisture codes track the drying of fuel layers of increasing depth, and three indices combine them with wind into a rating of fire behaviour. FWI is a daily index, computed from the weather at noon. See References.

Model versions (model_version):

  • cffdrs: the standard daily system, with the equations and constants of the cffdrs R package and tested against its published values. It steps at each cell's local standard noon (time zone from the cell's position, no daylight saving time), with the noon weather interpolated from the hourly inputs and the rain accumulated since the previous noon.
  • legacy: the formulation of the Italian operational chain: noon in local civil time, daily step computed when the output is written.
  • sliding_window: computed on rolling 24-hour windows instead of at noon.

Static data: a domain mask. Warm state: yes. Write one map per day with output_time_resolution: 24; with cffdrs, set output_time_offset to the hours from the run date at which every cell of the domain has passed its noon (for example 12 for a domain east of Greenwich).

Variable Meaning ffmc Fine Fuel Moisture Code: moisture of litter and fine fuel dmc Duff Moisture Code: moisture of loosely compacted organic layers dc Drought Code: moisture of deep, compact organic layers isi Initial Spread Index: expected rate of spread bui Build-Up Index: total fuel available fwi Fire Weather Index: overall fire intensity rating ifwi IFWI, a non-linear rescaling of fwi

docs.title: Other indices
docs.text:
These indices read their cells from a text file (cells_file_path, see Input Data) instead of GeoTIFF layers. Those with memory keep their warm state in text files (warm_state_path).

type Index Origin Variables Warm state KBDI Keetch–Byram Drought Index United States kbdi (mm of soil water deficit) yes Mark5 McArthur Forest Fire Danger Index, Mark 5 Australia df drought factor, ffdi yes Angstrom Angström index Sweden angstrom no Fosberg Fosberg Fire Weather Index United States ffwi no Nesterov Nesterov ignition index Russia nesterov yes Sharples Sharples fuel moisture and fire danger Australia fmi, f no Orieux Orieux water reserve and danger class France pet_t (mm), orieux_wr (mm), orieux_fd (class 0–3) yes Hdw Hot–Dry–Windy Index United States hdw no

docs.title: Input Data
docs.text: A run needs two kinds of data: weather inputs, which change at every run, and static data, which you prepare once for your domain. This page describes the format of both. The sample data is a complete, small example of each.

docs.title: Weather inputs
docs.text: Weather inputs are NetCDF files (NetCDF-4 or classic) in one directory. Every .nc file in it is read; a run can mix files, for example one per variable or one per forecast day, as long as each file carries its own coordinates and time axis.

docs.title: File layout
docs.text:
Each file holds:

  • a time variable: one value per timestamp, with a CF units attribute such as hours since 2025-07-01 00:00:00 (without the attribute, seconds since 1970-01-01 are assumed);
  • latitude and longitude variables with two dimensions (y, x), giving the position of each grid point in degrees (WGS84);
  • the weather variables, with dimensions (time, y, x).
dimensions:
    time = 744 ;  y = 11 ;  x = 24 ;
variables:
    int64 time(time) ;          time:units = "seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00" ;
    float latitude(y, x) ;
    float longitude(y, x) ;
    float T(time, y, x) ;       T:units = "degC" ;
    float H(time, y, x) ;
    ...

The grid can be regular or curvilinear and can have any resolution: each model cell takes the value of the nearest grid point. Missing values are written as -9999.

Files with one-dimensional coordinates

Many datasets store latitude(latitude) and longitude(longitude) as 1-D axes. Expand them to 2-D before a run, for example with xarray:

import numpy as np, xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_dataset("forecast.nc").rename({"latitude": "y", "longitude": "x"})
lon, lat = np.meshgrid(ds.x.values, ds.y.values)
ds = ds.assign(latitude=(("y", "x"), lat), longitude=(("y", "x"), lon))
ds.to_netcdf("input/forecast.nc")

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Name each variable as in the first column. Give the ones your models need; the others can be left out.

Name Meaning Units T Air temperature at 2 m °C or K (detected) H Relative humidity at 2 m % R Dew point temperature at 2 m, instead of H °C or K Q, PSFC Specific humidity and surface pressure, instead of H kg/kg, Pa W, D Wind speed at 10 m and the direction it blows from m/s, degrees U, V Wind components at 10 m, instead of W and D m/s P Rain fallen since the previous timestamp mm SNOW Snow cover depth cm K, F, O Observed temperature, humidity and rain, alternatives to T, H, P as above NDVI, NDWI, M, SWI Satellite vegetation, water, moisture and soil water indices –

Use hourly timestamps for RISICO: it is built for hourly steps, and rain must be the amount of the step, not an accumulation since the start of the forecast. Which variables each model uses is listed in Fire Danger Indices.

docs.title: Other variable names
docs.text:
If your files use other names, map them in the configuration with a netcdf_input_configuration section at the top level:

netcdf_input_configuration:
  lat_name: lat              # name of the latitude variable
  lon_name: lon              # name of the longitude variable
  time_name: valid_time      # name of the time variable
  variable_map:
    - { internal_name: T, name: t2m }
    - { internal_name: H, name: rh2m }
    - { internal_name: P, name: tp_hourly, offset: -3600 }

offset, in seconds, shifts the time axis of one variable: for example -3600 when the rain of the hour ending at 13:00 is stored at 13:00 but should be read at 12:00. Two optional keys handle unusual files: time_units names the attribute that holds the time units, when it is not units, and coords_dims (a pair of dimension names) selects the latitude and longitude dimensions when the coordinate variables have more than two.

docs.title: Legacy zbin inputs
docs.text: Instead of a directory, the input argument can be a text file listing .zbin files, one per line: the binary format of the previous RISICO implementation. New setups should use NetCDF.

docs.title: Static data
docs.text:
Static data describe the land on the grid the model computes on. They are single-band GeoTIFF files, all with exactly the same grid:

  • geographic coordinates (EPSG:4326), north up, not rotated;
  • the same number of rows and columns and the same pixel size and origin.
Layer Content Needed by Domain mask Non-zero on the cells to compute, 0 or nodata elsewhere. It defines the model grid. every model with static_data Slope Terrain slope, degrees RISICO Aspect Direction the slope faces, degrees clockwise from north RISICO Vegetation id Vegetation type of each cell, an id of the vegetation catalogue RISICO PPF summer, PPF winter Seasonal weights of spread and intensity (optional, both or neither) RISICO

Slope and aspect are usually derived from a digital elevation model, for example with gdaldem slope and gdaldem aspect; the vegetation id from a land-cover map reclassified to the catalogue's ids.

docs.title: Vegetation catalogue
docs.text:
A whitespace-separated text file with one line per vegetation type. The first line is a header and starts with #:

#ID d0  d1  hhv    umid   v0   T0     sat  use_ndvi     decodifica
0   0   0   -9999  -9999  0    -9999 -9999 false        non vegetato
1   0.5 0   17000  -9999  84   12     40   true         praterie_bassa_susc
Column Meaning Units ID Value used in the vegetation-id layer – d0 Dead fine fuel load kg/m² d1 Live fuel load kg/m² hhv Higher heating value of the fuel kJ/kg umid Moisture of the live fuel % v0 Base rate of spread, with no wind, slope or drying m/h T0 Time the dead fuel takes to respond to the weather h sat Moisture of the dead fuel when saturated % use_ndvi Whether the satellite NDVI modulates this type true/false last column Description –

-9999 marks a value that does not apply. The sample data ships the catalogue used for Italy (p_vegetazione.csv).

docs.title: Cell files for the other indices
docs.text:
The indices other than RISICO and FWI (KBDI, Mark 5, Angström and others, see Fire Danger Indices) read their cells from a text file instead of GeoTIFF layers: one line per cell with longitude, latitude and a third value, separated by spaces. The third value is the mean annual rainfall in mm for KBDI and Mark 5, the heat index for Orieux, and is ignored by the others.

8.900 44.400 1100
8.910 44.400 1100

docs.title: Programmatic Workflow
docs.text: The models are a Rust library, risico, separate from the risico-2023 runner: every index is a pure computation on arrays of cells, with no files involved. Use it to embed RISICO in another program, run it on cells you already hold in memory, or test a formulation. This guide shows the model API; the full item-by-item documentation is in the API Reference.

docs.title: Add the dependency
docs.text:
The library is published as the risico-2023 crate. Without the default build-binary feature it leaves out the runner's dependencies (NetCDF, GeoTIFF, Zarr, CLI):

[dependencies]
risico-2023 = { git = "https://github.com/CIMAFoundation/risico-2023", branch = "dev", default-features = false }
chrono = "0.4"

The crate is imported as risico. Add the config feature for the configuration.yml schema types (risico::config).

docs.title: The model API
docs.text:
Every model in risico::modules is made of the same pieces:

Piece Type What it holds Properties RISICOProperties, FWIProperties, ... What does not change during a run, one element per cell: coordinates, and for RISICO slope, aspect, vegetation and PPF Warm state RISICOWarmState, FWIWarmState, ... The per-cell memory a run starts from and saves at its end State RISICOState, FWIState, ... The running state, created from the warm state and a start time Input models::input::Input The weather of one timestamp on every cell Output models::output::Output The variables computed at one timestamp, read by OutputVariableName

Properties, states and inputs are aligned arrays: element i of each is the same cell.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
The library has its own units; the runner converts the input files to them:

Quantity Unit Temperature °C Relative humidity % Wind speed m/h Wind direction radians, the direction the wind comes from Rain mm Snow cover cm Slope, aspect radians

Missing values are risico::constants::NODATAVAL. InputElement::default() fills every field with it, so set the variables a model needs and leave the others.

docs.title: Stepping each model
docs.text:
The runner drives each model with the same calls in every tile; follow the same order:

Model Every timestamp When an output is wanted RISICO state.update(&props, &input) state.output(&props, &input) FWI state.update(&props, &input) state.output(&props) Mark 5 state.store(&input, &props) state.output(&props), once a day KBDI, Orieux state.store(&input) state.update(&props) then state.output(), once a day Nesterov state.store(&input, &props) state.update() then state.output(), once a day Angström, Fosberg, Sharples, HDW state.store(&input) state.output()

FWI steps at local standard noon: call FWIProperties::compute_standard_offsets once before the run.

docs.title: RISICO on one cell
docs.text:
examples/risico_single_cell.rs runs RISICO for two days of synthetic weather and prints the fine fuel moisture, rate of spread and intensity every six hours:

use std::{collections::HashMap, f32::consts::PI, sync::Arc};

use chrono::{Duration, TimeZone, Utc};
use risico::{
    models::{
        input::{Input, InputElement},
        output::OutputVariableName,
    },
    modules::risico::{
        config::RISICOModelConfig,
        models::{
            RISICOCellPropertiesContainer, RISICOProperties, RISICOState, RISICOVegetation,
            RISICOWarmState,
        },
    },
};

fn main() {
    // One cell: position, terrain and vegetation. The vegetation parameters
    // normally come from the catalogue CSV; the default is a generic fuel.
    let vegetation = Arc::new(RISICOVegetation::default());
    let properties = RISICOProperties::new(
        RISICOCellPropertiesContainer {
            lons: vec![8.86],
            lats: vec![44.45],
            slopes: vec![5.0_f32.to_radians()],
            aspects: vec![160.0_f32.to_radians()],
            vegetations: vec![vegetation.clone()],
        },
        HashMap::from([(vegetation.id.clone(), vegetation)]),
        vec![1.0], // summer PPF
        vec![1.0], // winter PPF
    );

    // Start from 40 % fine fuel moisture, the default warm state.
    let start = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2026, 7, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();
    let mut state = RISICOState::new(&[RISICOWarmState::default()], &start, RISICOModelConfig::new("v2025"));

    for hour in 1..=48 {
        let time = start + Duration::hours(hour);
        let phase = 2.0 * PI * ((hour as f32 - 15.0) / 24.0);
        // Units are the library's own: wind speed in m/h, direction in radians.
        let weather = InputElement {
            temperature: 26.0 + 6.0 * phase.cos(),
            humidity: 45.0 - 20.0 * phase.cos(),
            wind_speed: 4.0 * 3600.0,
            wind_dir: 270.0_f32.to_radians(),
            rain: 0.0,
            snow_cover: 0.0,
            ..InputElement::default()
        };
        let input = Input { time, data: vec![weather].into() };

        state.update(&properties, &input);
        if hour % 6 == 0 {
            let output = state.output(&properties, &input);
            let value = |name| output.get(&name).unwrap()[0];
            println!(
                "{time}  dffm {:5.1} %  V {:6.1} m/h  I {:7.1} kW/m",
                value(OutputVariableName::dffm),
                value(OutputVariableName::V),
                value(OutputVariableName::I),
            );
        }
    }
}

$ cargo run --release --example risico_single_cell
2026-07-01 06:00:00 UTC  dffm  35.7 %  V    7.1 m/h  I    10.6 kW/m
2026-07-01 12:00:00 UTC  dffm  30.8 %  V   17.7 m/h  I    28.7 kW/m
2026-07-01 18:00:00 UTC  dffm  25.7 %  V   41.4 m/h  I    73.3 kW/m
...
2026-07-03 00:00:00 UTC  dffm  12.7 %  V  139.6 m/h  I   298.9 kW/m

RISICOModelConfig::new selects the formulation: legacy, v2023 or v2025.

docs.title: Vegetation
docs.text:
RISICOVegetation holds one row of the vegetation catalogue (p_vegetazione.csv):

Field Meaning id, name Identifier in the vegetation-id layer, description d0, d1 Dead fine fuel load, live fuel load hhv Higher heating value [kJ/kg] umid Live fuel moisture v0 Base rate of spread [m/h] T0 Response time of the dead fine fuel moisture [h] sat Saturation moisture of the dead fine fuel [%] use_ndvi Whether satellite NDVI modulates the live fuel

docs.title: FWI on one cell
docs.text:
examples/fwi_single_cell.rs runs the Canadian FWI System for five days of hourly weather and prints the codes at noon:

use chrono::{Duration, TimeZone, Utc};
use risico::{
    models::{
        input::{Input, InputElement},
        output::OutputVariableName,
    },
    modules::fwi::{
        config::FWIModelConfig,
        models::{FWICellPropertiesContainer, FWIProperties, FWIState, FWIWarmState},
    },
};

fn main() {
    let start = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2026, 7, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap();

    let mut properties = FWIProperties::new(FWICellPropertiesContainer {
        lons: vec![8.86],
        lats: vec![44.45],
    });
    // FWI steps at local standard noon: resolve each cell's UTC offset once.
    properties.compute_standard_offsets(&start);

    // A warm state is a short history of codes; start from the standard
    // FFMC 85, DMC 6, DC 15 the day before.
    let warm_state = FWIWarmState {
        dates: vec![start - Duration::days(1)],
        ffmc: vec![85.0],
        dmc: vec![6.0],
        dc: vec![15.0],
        rain: vec![0.0],
    };
    let mut state = FWIState::new(&[warm_state], &start, FWIModelConfig::new("legacy"));

    for hour in 1..=5 * 24 {
        let time = start + Duration::hours(hour);
        let weather = InputElement {
            temperature: 28.0,
            humidity: 30.0,
            wind_speed: 5.0 * 3600.0, // m/h
            rain: 0.0,
            ..InputElement::default()
        };
        state.update(&properties, &Input { time, data: vec![weather].into() });

        if hour % 24 == 12 {
            let output = state.output(&properties);
            let value = |name| output.get(&name).unwrap()[0];
            println!(
                "{time}  FFMC {:5.1}  DMC {:5.1}  DC {:6.1}  ISI {:4.1}  BUI {:5.1}  FWI {:4.1}",
                value(OutputVariableName::ffmc),
                value(OutputVariableName::dmc),
                value(OutputVariableName::dc),
                value(OutputVariableName::isi),
                value(OutputVariableName::bui),
                value(OutputVariableName::fwi),
            );
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Many cells
docs.text:
Nothing changes for a grid: pass one element per cell in every vector, and one InputElement per cell in each Input. update and output process the cells in parallel with ndarray's Zip. The risico-2023 runner does exactly this on tiles of the domain, so memory stays bounded however large the domain is (see Large Domains and Performance).

To save and restore a run, map the state's cells back to warm-state records (for RISICO, the dffm, snow and satellite fields of each RISICOStateElement) and pass them to State::new next time.

docs.title: References
docs.text: The scientific publications behind the models in risico-2023.

docs.title: RISICO
docs.text:
• Fiorucci, P., Gaetani, F., Minciardi, R. (2008). Development and application of a system for dynamic wildfire risk assessment in Italy. Environmental Modelling & Software, 23(6), 690–702. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2007.05.008

    The original description of RISICO: the fuel moisture and fire spread models, run on every grid cell at every forecast step, from limited-area weather forecasts and maps of vegetation and terrain.

  • Perello, N., Trucchia, A., D'Andrea, M., Meschi, G., Ghasemiazma, F., Degli Esposti, S., Fiorucci, P., Ferraris, L., Gollini, A., Negro, D. (2025). Fuel-aware forest fire danger rating system RISICO: a comparative study for Italy. International Journal of Wildland Fire, 34, WF25023. doi:10.1071/WF25023 (open access)

    The current version of the model, with fuel classes derived from a machine-learning wildfire susceptibility map, compared with other fire danger indices on 16 years of Italian wildfires.

docs.title: Building the Web Demo
docs.text:
The interactive demo runs the unmodified risico-2023 binary, compiled for the WASI target:

rustup target add wasm32-wasip1
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip1 --bin risico-2023
cp target/wasm32-wasip1/release/risico-2023.wasm docs/demo/

The docs workflow does the same on every push to dev and main, so the bundle is never committed.

docs.title: What differs on WASI
docs.text:
The WASI build is the same program with a few platform switches:

  • Zarr output is not available: zarrs and its zstd dependency do not build for WASI. The demo writes NetCDF only.
  • NetCDF files are read into memory where the reader has no positioned file access (open_netcdf in src/bin/common/io/mod.rs).
  • No threads: there is no tile pool and rayon runs on the calling thread.
  • The temporary directory is $TMPDIR (or /tmp) and the process id is 0.

docs.title: How the page runs it
docs.text:
docs/demo/ holds a static page and a few ES modules:

File Role app.html, app.js The page: map, controls, charts, map rendering worker.js Runs the binary in a Web Worker lib/runner.js Builds an in-memory filesystem with @bjorn3/browser_wasi_shim, runs the binary, collects its files lib/scenario.js Turns a scenario into configuration.yml, static layers, cell lists and arguments lib/netcdf3.js Writes the weather input as a NetCDF classic file lib/geotiff-write.js Writes the domain mask and static layers as GeoTIFFs lib/openmeteo.js Fetches hourly weather from Open-Meteo

The outputs are the binary's own NetCDF-4 files, read with h5wasm. The shim grows a file by reallocating it on every write; runner.js replaces that with a doubling buffer, which cut the time spent writing outputs by a factor of five on a run over the whole of Italy.

The static layers the page loads (docs/demo/data/static/) are a cut-out of the 1 km Italian domain around Liguria (7.40–10.20 °E, 43.70–44.75 °N, 274 × 103 cells): domain mask, slope, aspect, vegetation id, PPF and the vegetation catalogue, plus the colour palettes in docs/demo/data/palettes/. docs/demo/data/sample/ holds the July 2025 weather the page uses by default (a NetCDF input, rebuilt by docs/demo/tools/make_sample_weather.py) and a configuration to run it with the command-line model. The page reads whatever grid the layers define, so a larger domain only needs other files; for one the size of Italy (317 000 cells) set a coarser Open-Meteo grid (COARSE, REFINE in app.js) and expect about a minute and 1.1 GB of browser memory.

docs.title: Testing locally
docs.text:
Serve docs/ with any static server that sends application/wasm for .wasm files:

python3 -m http.server --directory docs 8765

and open http://127.0.0.1:8765/demo/app.html. mkdocs serve works too and shows the page inside the documentation.
